questions.prompt: **Two Sum.** Return the indices of the two numbers in `nums` that add up to `target`, smaller index first. Exactly one answer exists, and you may not use the same element twice. Aim for O(n).
questions.explanation: Store each value's index as you go and look up the complement `target - nums[i]` before adding the current value, which is what makes { 3, 3 } work. One pass, O(n) time and space.

questions.prompt: **Valid parentheses.** Return true if every bracket in `s` (only `()[]{}`) is closed by the same type, in the right order.
questions.explanation: A stack holds the brackets still waiting to be closed; each closer must match the most recent opener. The two edge cases people miss: a closer when the stack is empty, and openers left over at the end.

questions.prompt: **Binary search.** `nums` is sorted ascending. Return the index of `target`, or -1 if it isn't there. O(log n).
questions.explanation: With an inclusive range [lo, hi] the loop condition is `lo <= hi` (otherwise a one-element range is skipped and the last element is missed), and both moves must step past mid. `lo + (hi - lo) / 2` avoids overflow on huge arrays.

questions.prompt: **Reverse a linked list.** Reverse the singly linked list starting at `head` and return the new head. Do it in place, in O(1) extra space.
questions.explanation: Walk the list keeping three references: the previous node, the current one and the next one. Save `next` before pointing the current node backwards, or you lose the rest of the list. At the end `prev` is the new head.

questions.prompt: **Maximum subarray.** Return the largest sum of any non-empty contiguous run of `nums`. O(n).
questions.explanation: Kadane's algorithm: the best run ending at i either extends the best run ending at i-1 or starts fresh at i. Starting `best` at 0 instead of nums[0] gets the all-negative case wrong.

questions.prompt: **Merge intervals.** Each interval is `[start, end]`. Merge all overlapping intervals (touching ones like [1,4] and [4,5] count as overlapping) and return them sorted by start.
questions.explanation: Sort by start, then each interval either overlaps the last merged one (extend its end) or starts a new one. Take the max of the ends: [1,10] followed by [2,3] must stay [1,10].

questions.prompt: **Valid anagram.** Return true if `t` uses exactly the same letters as `s`, the same number of times each.
questions.explanation: Count letters in one string and count them back down with the other: O(n). Checking only that each letter appears (a set) wrongly accepts "aab" vs "abb". Sorting both strings also works, in O(n log n).

questions.prompt: **Longest substring without repeating characters.** Return the length of the longest substring of `s` in which no character appears twice. O(n).
questions.explanation: Keep a window [start, i] with no repeats. When s[i] was last seen inside the window, move start just past it. The classic bug is moving start backwards to an occurrence that's already outside the window, which "abba" catches.

questions.prompt: **Climbing stairs.** You can climb 1 or 2 steps at a time. Return how many distinct ways there are to climb `n` steps (1 ≤ n ≤ 45). The last test needs an efficient solution.
questions.explanation: Ways(n) = Ways(n-1) + Ways(n-2), because the last move was a 1-step or a 2-step: it's Fibonacci. Plain recursion makes billions of calls for n = 45 and times out; keep only the last two values (or memoise).

questions.prompt: **Group anagrams.** Group the words that are anagrams of each other. Groups and the words inside them can be in any order.
questions.explanation: Anagrams have the same letters in sorted order, so use that as a dictionary key. O(n · k log k) for n words of length k; a 26-letter count as the key makes it O(n · k).

questions.prompt: **Top K frequent elements.** Return the `k` most frequent numbers in `nums`, in any order. The answer is unique.
questions.explanation: Count with a dictionary, then keep the k largest counts in a size-k min-heap: O(n log k). Sorting all counts is O(n log n) and also passes; bucket sort by count gets O(n).

questions.prompt: **Number of islands.** `grid` is made of '1' (land) and '0' (water). An island is land connected up, down, left or right (not diagonally). Return how many islands there are.
questions.explanation: Scan the grid; each unvisited '1' starts a new island, and a flood fill (DFS or BFS) marks all of its land as visited. O(rows × cols). The diagonal test checks that only four directions connect.
